# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. I just saw Coyote Vs Acme today

**Score:** 115
**Body:** This movie went through hell to get here today but in maybe one of the rarest cases of its kind the film is actually incredible.

The rotten tomatoes score could have been a ton of critics just happy to see a film like this finally make it to theatres rather than praising the overall film but man I am so glad that's not the case.

It just released in the UK yesterday and I just got back from seeing it just now.

I genuinely couldn't stop smiling through the whole film. Each new scene I just couldn't wrap my head around how this almost got deleted..... then I remembered the CEO allegedly didn't even watch the film.

The score, the cinematography, the writing. The animation work. How is it a home run on everything? I'm really at a loss for words how good this movie turned out to be.

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. This is somehow my most anticipated US release of 2026, and I can’t wait to see it soon! As funny as it feels to say on this sub, I thought that *Looney Tunes: Back in Action* was a lot of fun and wonderfully made, and I’m expecting something similar from *Coyote vs. Acme*.
2. I thought it was really great. I thought it pissed-from-a-great-height on all of the Disney 'live-action' reboots/legacy sequels in terms of revisiting, reinterrogating and reinterpreting the original material, the legacy of the 'IP' an the 'problematic' elements in an interesting and entertaining way. Even the obligatory 'nostalgia-bait' stuff (Daffy, Bugs sections etc) I thought were really well executed - or maybe I just think that because the pandering worked on me hahaha. That said it speaks to how I was really drawn in by it on an emotional level!

I loved the reinterpretation of Wile E. Coyote's Roadrunner chasing as a Sisyphusean endeavour, and that one of the most famous pop interpretations of the myth (Camus' "one must imagine Sisyphus happy") was able to be implied and left unspoken in the text. That in the face of corporate hegemony, corporal exploitation and (seeming?) subjugation as a class, and against the huge amount of effort and trauma required of navigating legal resistance to those things, Wile E. simply longs to go about his task by any means and live free (and 'wild' as the animal that he truly is outside of the 'toon' context.)

I found the Foghorn Leghorn interpretation really interesting. He's a CEO and has apparently been allowed to ascend to a level we see from few other toon characters (and the only non-human toon character in a high social status at all), but he regularly has 'microagressions' (for want of a better term) inflicted on him by the Cena character, and is viewed as having 'succeeded' in the courtroom only by causing himself cartoon physical injury, debasing himself in front of humans and reifying the social role of a Toon character, indicating his acceptance by the ruling class may not be as solid or sincere as it seems. Honestly, it make me think of minstrelsy and Spike Lee's *Bamboozled -* Leghorn as a kind of class traitor or Uncle Tom figure I guess. Truly fascinating and maybe wish we had a little more of that

## 2. The lighthouse island is alive. (The Lighthouse 2019 Film Interpretation/Theory)

**Score:** 21
**Body:** I'm about 7 years too late, I know, but I haven't seen this theory float around film spaces yet. After my 4th viewing yesterday, I came to this conclusion about the film.

  
The island in The Lighthouse (2019) is a sentient prison-like entity. Not in any real or biological sense but in the sense that it's a supernatural place built to serve a punitive function. This idea used in horror is similar to the hotel in The Shining or Monster House. I believe it is a self sustaining prison that beckons the guilty (with the thought that they're voluntarily going there of their own volition) and enslaves, imprisons, and punishes them with madness. The island facilitates this as a way of sustaining itself and its light through their labor. All aspects of the area play a role in damning/punishing the keepers/prisoners of it. The seagulls, incessant storms, false prospects of women and parole (The boats never coming to save them). The island dangles mercy in front of them without ever actually granting it. Much like the myth of Prometheus when he is regenerated everyday just for his abdomen to be eaten again and again, giving Prometheus respite and false hopes of a halting of the punishment.

  
Dafoe, who is a veteran of the island, acquires a warden-like role. Functioning as some sort of pseudo right hand man. He brings new inmates to punish, assigns them duties to maintain the island, belittles them, etc. Despite his role though, he still suffers by the island's hand, yet another false mercy by being led to believe he has any real power.

  
Pattinson, whose stained past led him to arrive there to look for legitimacy, is hopeful for lightwatching duties but is rejected instantly by Dafoe. I believe the light represents the prospect of redemption and freedom, like moths and flames. Dafoe's obsession with it is an intentional result of the island, to keep him there as he is a prisoner and the warden. He was deceived by the light to become an extension of the island and an integral part to keeping the light and life of it.

  
Now, to answer a question that plagued me on all my watches. Why was Dafoe allowed to look inside the light but Pattinson wasn't? I think I finally understand why (atleast relative to my theory). I believe the island rewards Dafoe of his patronage by allowing him to derive pleasure from the light with the ulterior motive of the island being to keep him there for as long as he lives, sort of like a life sentence. When Pattinson looked inside after murdering Dafoe, he was punished with eternal Promethean wrath because he had killed the island's trusted keeper. And moreso, the island deems viewing the light undeservedly as a transgression, and Pattinson died because he did not accept the truth behind his guilt while Dafoe did. While it is unclear what exactly it was that Dafoe had done to deserve imprisonment, I think he is accepting of his guilt (which I think is the another goal of the prison). However, It is implied that Dafoe killed Pattinson's precedessor because he also tried to undeservedly access the light, an act that I believe was permitted by the island because it deemed it to be a fitting punishment.

  
An extra idea that reinforces my theory is the subtle scene of repressed homosexuality (You know which one). When they almost succumb to the loneliness and kiss each other, they quickly wake up to what they're doing and instead express that passion through fistfighting. A familiar case which alludes to the guise of masculinity to veil and repress the true sexuality of those in denial. A case that is ever present in prison.

  
Thoughts?

 

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Dafoe in part surely symbolises Proteus, the "Old Man of the Sea" as Homer described. 

Pattinson indeed in part symbolises Prometheus, and surely then him gazing at "the light" is Prometheus stealing "the fire" from the gods? 

I think your reading is fun and valid, but I don't think it's Eggers intended explanation. In fact, I've heard him say the film is a purposefully layered metaphor with no deliberate single meaning. It is a story unto itself, and the various metaphysical and mythological images are to portray to us the feeling and experience of the madness of these men, there is no 'key' to 'unlock' it. 
  - Tbh i think op is valuing Egger's intentions by sharing their own interpretation. It doesn't seem like they're trying to assert their theory as "the" explanation for the film, just offering a possible explanation, another reading to approach the film with.
  - I wholeheartedly agree that the film is undoubtedly a huge allusion to greek mythology, in many aspects. But I find that in those aspects, it doesnt encompass the themes of the film as a whole. I think the greek portion is not wholly incompatible with my prison theory and the two can coexist in the films canon
2. Fun read. Thanks for writing this, OP.

I don’t have anything to add other than to say it’s definitely my favorite from that director. Easily his most interesting film and I appreciate its strangeness, its sense of humor and horror, and its audacity. 

## 3. The Cautionary Tale of Richard Stanley

**Score:** 2
**Body:** There is an excellent documentary about Richard Stanley’s disastrous experience adapting the HG Wells The Island of Dr Moreau called Lost Souls. It’s a deep look into the pitfalls of developing and producing your lifelong dream project. Also directing Marlon Brando or Val Kilmer as well! I wrote a substack article about the story if that’s more interesting than documentaries for you. I work in film (was a development exec then rewrites) and it’s very relatable and frankly depressing. 

I find these documentaries that follow doomed projects strangely fascinating, like a car accident but worse. I’ve never experienced a set or development on this level. Have any of you? I’d love to hear what you learned from the experience, and if you went back for more?

https://notesonfilmdevelopment.substack.com/p/the-director-who-lost-his-own-movie?r=4idcqp&utm\_medium=ios

### Top 1 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. It seems like they picked the rainforests of Far North Queensland because they looked cool and did literally no other research, which I find incredible. I doubt a single Australian would have recommend filming in the rainforest, during cyclone season, in an area with one of the largest saltwater crocodile populations on earth.

## 4. [SPOILER ALERT] Discussion on THE OTHERS (2001)

**Score:** 0
**Body:** [SPOILER ALERT] 

Why didn't the amazing twist in 'The Others' didn't really feel like a shock? It felt more like a copy from sixth sense?

I had no clue, whatsoever, about the movie when I started watching it. 

Watched The Others for the first time recently, and when the truth came out, first with the servants, then with protagonist and the kids, I didn't get that jolt I was expecting. No shock, no "wait, what just happened." Just a kind of flat acknowledgment: "oh, the protagonist is dead," which felt like a direct lift from The Sixth Sense.

And that's the weird part, because Sixth Sense actually blew my mind when I first saw it. Cole never directly interacting with Malcolm, the cold spots, all those clues you don't clock until the reveal, it worked because I had no idea what was coming. With The Others, I went in without spoilers too, but I was still kind of indifferent by the time the reveal hit. It felt like I'd already seen this movie two years earlier.

Maybe it's just that The Sixth Sense got there first and made the "character doesn't know they're dead" twist a known device, so anything using it afterward loses the element of surprise. Or maybe The Others leans so heavily on the same structure, isolated house, oddly behaving side characters, the slow dawning realization, that it just can't help but feel derivative rather than original.

Surprised I haven't seen more discussion connecting the two. Anyone else feel this way, or did The Others actually land for you?

### Top 3 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. If you visit [this link](https://scripts-onscreen.com/movie/the-others-script-links/) you can see there’s a draft script dated 1998 - before The Sixth Sense came out. I’ve not gone through the script but apparently it and other Spanish drafts (it was originally intended to be a Spanish-language film) have the same plot as the eventual film

You can also see [this article](https://elpais.com/diario/1999/07/28/cultura/933112807_850215.html). It’s not English language, but you can see that not only is it talking about the film (the words “the Others” appear), but that it is far enough along that Nicole Kidman is attached (or, from my reading, is rumoured to be attached but hasn’t been confirmed). That article is from 4 months before The Sixth Sense came out

So, I don’t think the idea of the protagonists being dead is lifted from the Sixth Sense. It’s integral to the story and is unquestionably not tacked on after the fact. It makes a lift improbable

As for which worked better, for me I thought The Others was more impactful as a twist. Perhaps it would have been different without the hype around The Sixth Sense and with a different advertising campaign, but I’d worked out the twist going in

All you need is four pieces of information, the all of which were in the trailer or part of the buzz around it: 

1. The film is about a boy who can see dead people

2. The people don’t know they’re dead

3. The film has conversations between Willis’ character and Osmet

4. There is a twist

Given just those pieces of information, what is the most logical thing to assume for the twist? And then Willis is shot in the first 5 minutes of the film

With The Others I had no idea, so it definitely hit me

The Others is very different emotionally, too. Willis was shot by a former patient and spends his afterlife trying to help someone. Grace killed her children
  - Yes true. 

Amazing response. 
2. The protagonist being dead/ghosts all along is not an idea introduced into cinema by Sixth sense anyway.

Carnival of Souls and Jacob's Ladder are movies that use that 19th century concept for their plot twists. Difference is, almost nobody watched those while everybody watched The Sixth Sense at the time.
3. I haven't seen this movie in a long time, but I recently read **The Turn of the Screw** by Henry James, which was part of the inspiration for the movie. There was a more straightforward adaptation of the book in the 60s, **The Innocents**, which is a great movie and is part of psychological horror canon. With these things in mind, I think The Others does an amazing job of applying that twist to change the story arc and resolution out of the adapted plot elements (in a satisfying way, imo)

## 5. Can a love of classic cinema and impatience with others' antipathy towards it be accounted for by one's own exposure (Or lack thereof) to certain media growing up? 

**Score:** 0
**Body:** I've flirted with the thought for years that the movies I watched and didn't watch growing up shaped how my tastes would eventually settle into their current form in a bit of a unique way. I was curious if anyone has experienced anything remotely similar. 

I skipped a lot of the 80s-90s blockbusters growing up (With some exceptions here and there like Ghostbusters and E.T. that I did catch), not seeing them until 2014-2016 in my late teens. At this same time, I was exploring cinema in general. While I was, to my own tremendous disappointment, disenchanted by Star Wars and Indiana Jones (Although I ended up loving Terminator and Back to the Future as if I HAD grown up with them, so I wasn't trying to be a snob by any means), I was exploring much older films and having a pretty radically different experience. I was simultaneously LOVING movies like Casablanca, All About Eve, Charade, My Man Godfrey, The Day the Earth Stood Still and Bride of Frankenstein. I still obsess over them over a decade later. 

What probably helped was that I went into cinema exploration with a bit of a bookworm's mindset, fully acclimatized to a slow burn and patience being necessary to get to the good stuff. I was noticing quickly how bringing up my enthusiasm for these movies to peers earned me baffled reactions and even harsh judgment and assumptions. I was so confused by this and in my younger years, unfortunately a bit judgemental in return to match their reactions to my findings.

I realized over time that I cannot expect people who likely did grow up with the exact movies I skipped to see the worth that I see. But man oh man, when you don't grow up on an 80s blockbuster diet, it's outstandingly obvious just how much Raiders of the Lost Ark is a strange combination of Lawrence of Arabia and old adventure serials, and not in a way that especially flatters it. Although as a counterpoint to that, apparently critics who obviously had no nostalgia for the film at the time did embrace it wholeheartedly, so maybe I am a snob. I found myself agreeing with Pauline Kael that if anything Temple of Doom did it better by leaning into the wackiness over trying to have your cake and eat it. Indiana Jones was always going to be more serial than Lawrence of Arabia, better face that rather than hide it. 

But anyway. I think growing up with pretty much every Disney movie minus the package films and Black Cauldron also primed me for loving classics, some of these movies being actually made in that era or else leaning on the grand musical tradition, as well as clear paragon leads and "God I love being evil" styled big bads. This connection I only realized just today and I wondered if there's a Disney-to-golden-age pipeline anyone else can perceive if not directly relate to. Animation in general is really friendly to older films, where instead of perfectly copying them in an attempt to "innovate" (My bias in putting that in quotation is not lost on me) they do such loving homages to them. I'm thinking of Animaniacs referencing everything from The Gold Rush to Seventh Seal, Cats Don't Dance incorporating Shirley Temple and Max from Sunset Boulevard, and the "Nosferatu!" gag in Spongebob. Having grown up with these things dear to my heart, it was almost inevitable I should prefer movies the ones I grew up on were throwing respect on and my impressionable brain was seeing.

So I suppose my theory is that rather than any inherent trait in a person that makes them appreciate classics over modern films more, what one is exposed or not exposed to as a child more closely informs what they'll gravitate to when they're older. But I'd love to know what you all think.

5. I don't think this is true. I didn't see a lot of classic film growing up. For many years I assumed that old movies would be full of characters I couldn't relate to. Sometime after college I saw ... probably \*Casablanca\*? and it blew my mind. Characters in old movies are the same type of flawed people as the characters in modern movies, and they're the same type of flawed people as everyone we know in real life, including ourselves. Other than the trans-Atlantic accent of old Hollywood, they talk the same way we do. They're not any less relatable now than they were then. Comedies are just as funny. Thrillers are just as thrilling. Dramas are just as moving.

I think that many people, though, do think the same way I thought then. It's a psychological barrier you, or at least some of us, have to overcome.

It doesn't help that people now are being exposed to film largely through streaming services, which tend not to highlight the wealth of classic film available. And I know it's trendy to hate on Marvel movies, and occasionally I enjoy one myself, but I am always shocked when I talk to coworkers who loved the latest dreck Marvel has turned out -- I remember when I said I didn't like \*Deadpool\* and one of them said, "But look at all the references!" This is, I know, a grumpy old man complaint, but it's like some viewers are totally unfamiliar with the concept that a movie could have substance or emotional weight.

8. I think it's just too simple of you. I grew up with 80s movies, 90s movies too, 2000s movies as well. Then I went hardcore into movies when I was a teenager in the 2010s, watched all the classics. My God, was I bored by old films. I could not stand them. They were too slow, too predictable. I was just bored by Casablanca. I didn't feel a thing watching a silent movie.

Some years later, after having seen so many movies of modern age, I sort of grew tired of Hollywood's formula. And suddenly the films that I was bored with, like Andrei Tarkovsky's movies, blew my mind away at a rewatch. Suddenly the old movies became my focus. Suddenly, because of my growing interest and appreciation in art, I started to fall in love with silent movies. Way Down East is one of my favorite films of all time now.

At the same time, I still like some fun action movies. Mind you, Tarkovsky loved Terminator, and Stanley Kubrick deeply respected Steven Spielberg for his vision.

I had a friend group where many used to binge-watching, only watching modern Netflix stuff basically. Well, one in that group, we started a project watching old, very old films for quite a while. At first, the disinterest was noticeable, just a mild curiosity. But with time, getting used to that storytelling vibe, starting to recognize actors and the language of film, man, they all got fucking into it. Even the most binge-prone person ever of the group, who had never even seen a black and white movie before, suddenly was super fucking down to watch five movies of Fantômas of the 1910s. Took time and patience and the will to get there, but they got there all right.

It is also, but not simply an acquired taste. It's more like they learned a new language. Their vocabulary expanded. Also, it was always an event, meeting to watch a film, and getting people to put in some actual dedication.

Simultaneously, Star Wars is far more than just a copy. It has so much personality. Hell, thinking of post-structuralism, everything is a mosaic of something that has already been done before or said before. The angle you get at, however, is a personal one. Your own language, your own view.

You can be a fucking phenomenal filmmaker, doing the most baffling movies, like today Bi Gan or Sion Sono, for example. You can also be someone who just fucking enjoys movies and almost does a sort of collage with a lot of personality, however, like Quentin Tarantino.

What matters is why you're doing it. You immediately notice when a film is just a cash grab. You notice when the artists don't really give a fuck. You immediately notice when they do, however. That's what I'm in for. (Though even the most blatant cash grab will usually have some passionate people giving their absolute all behind the scenes.)

People's tastes are not simply fixed. Very often you do not inherently dislike an art form. You just haven't learned its language, and, on that note, not found your niche in it yet. And I won't watch a Béla Tarr film with the same eyes as a Michael Bay movie. I try to meet the film on its own term, being a visitor experiencing someone's dream, and if it works for me, great; if not, oh well.
